new_statements.rule_in_words: Endle gives a layered, impressionistic rule set: by default stress falls on the first syllable and ignores vowel length (mo'sá); in words of three or more syllables it is 'as a general rule' penultimate; but his own rule-2 example fai'dangman (3 syllables, initial) is a verb, and rule 5 says verbs keep their root (first-syllable) accent through conjugation, compound verbs accent the second member, and prefixed/polysyllabic verb roots accent the second syllable (ga-glai'-nŭ); gă- adjectives accent the second syllable; nouns shift accent rightward under case suffixes (Mo'sá > Mosá'ni); enclitics nŭ, sŭi pull the accent onto the syllable just before them. Read together this looks like root-syllable prominence with penultimate placement in suffixed/longer words, but the source states it as 'initial' plus 'penultimate' plus exceptions, and never mentions tone although modern Boro is analysed as a two-tone language, so Endle's 'accent' may partly be pitch.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 6: long words carry a main accent (double mark) and a secondary accent (single mark), e.g. Tháng'-ni-áu''-nŭ 'even while going' — main accent on the third syllable, secondary on the first, 'the voice seeming to rest on it to gain strength for the utterance of a long word'.
new_statements.exceptions: gă- adjectives: second syllable accented (găzá', găfút'), first vowel 'very short', almost gzá; nouns may move accent from 1st to 2nd syllable when case endings are added (Mo'sá / Mosá'ni); verbs retain first-syllable accent in conjugation, but compound verbs accent the second member (khàt-láng'-bai) and verbal roots of more than one syllable accent the second syllable (ga-glai'-nŭ, ge-le'-nŭ); enclitics nŭ, sŭi cause the accent to rest on the immediately preceding syllable (ga-glai-nai'-sŭi); free variation noted for Gadat'/Gădet' etc. with first syllable suppressible.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level 'cadence' of citation/orthographic forms in Endle's romanization for Darrang Kachári; the accent domain includes case suffixes and enclitics (accent shifts before them). Impressionistic 19th-c. missionary description; no instrumental basis; tone not discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog kach1279 'Kachari' [xac] is anchored on Endle 1884, which describes the 'Kachári (Bårå)' of Darrang district, Assam — the speech LSI III-2 (1903: 5) took as the standard form of Bârâ/Bodo. That variety is what is today called Boro/Bodo (Glottolog sister languoid bodo1269); ISO xac now denotes a shifting remnant 'Kachari' population in Assam. Modern descriptions of Boro (Joseph & Burling 2006: 17-19, Kokrajhar; Das & Mahanta 2019) analyse it as a two-tone language with no clear word stress, whereas Endle never mentions tone, so his 'accent' rules may partly encode pitch. Not to be confused with Dimasa / 'Hill Kachari' (dima1251; Dundas 1908, Jacquesson), which the earlier scan note had drifted to.

sources.citation: Das, Kalyan & Shakuntala Mahanta. 2019. Intonational phonology of Boro. Glossa: a journal of general linguistics 4(1): 103, 1-35. DOI 10.5334/gjgl.758.
sources.note: Boro (bodo1269): two lexical tones, Prosodic Word is the tone domain; p. 3: 'As far as Boro is concerned... the attributes of stress are also not entirely clear and therefore Boro is not amenable to an analysis as a pitch-accent language'. No word-stress rule; context only (different glottocode).

sources.citation: Joseph, U. V. & Robbins Burling. 2006. The comparative phonology of the Boro-Garo languages. Mysore: Central Institute of Indian Languages. Boro section pp. 12-19 (archive.org dli.language.0865).
sources.note: Describes modern Boro (Kokrajhar; = bodo1269, the language Endle's 'Plains Kachari' is now subsumed) as having a two-way high/low tone contrast, one tone per word; no statement about word stress in Boro.
